extracted.intended_audience: judges, administrative-law practitioners, agency lawyers, and administrative-law scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and standards for when courts should defer to executive-branch agencies' statutory interpretations (the Chevron regime), including exceptions, historical practice, and stare-decisis considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency competence presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts confront statutory ambiguity, an agency to which Congress has delegated policymaking responsibilities may rely on an accountable actor’s views of wise policy to inform its judgments; decisions often involve the agency’s subject-matter expertise, regulatory experience, and policy choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use agency deference where the question implicates technical knowledge, long engagement with a regulatory scheme, or policy trade-offs (e.g., reconciling environmental protection versus economic growth; deciding how many flights over Grand Canyon are consistent with restoring natural quiet). Quote: “the decision is likely to involve the agency’s subject-matter expertise; to fall within its sphere of regulatory experience; and to involve policy choice.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron default rule (two-step presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress has not spoken clearly on an issue, apply a default rule that favors agency primacy in filling statutory gaps: first determine whether Congress addressed the issue; if not, defer to the agency’s reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize Chevron as a presumption Congress normally would want when it delegates regulatory power; courts should step back when Congress is silent and the issue falls within the agency’s delegated authority. The dissent emphasizes that Chevron asks what Congress would generally want when it leaves gaps, and that Congress rarely says otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts determine whether Congress has spoken
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts alone use normal interpretive tools to decide if Congress has addressed a given issue; only when courts find silence or ambiguity does a choice between court and agency arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ordinary tools of statutory interpretation at Chevron step one; defer to agencies only when courts conclude Congress has not resolved the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference when agency is not responsible for administering the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency gets no Chevron deference when construing a statute it is not charged with administering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis as supporting precedent: if Congress has not put the agency in charge of implementing a statute, the agency should not receive a special role in its construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference when agency bypasses required procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency will not receive deference if it reached its decision without using—or without properly using—its rulemaking or adjudicatory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: United States v. Mead Corp., Encino Motorcars v. Navarro. Rationale: Congress expects authoritative pronouncements to come from procedures enacted to foster fairness and deliberation; failure to follow those procedures undermines entitlement to deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deference in extraordinary cases of vast economic or political significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has declined to defer in cases involving questions of vast economic and political significance on the theory that Congress would not have left such matters to an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite King v. Burwell; treat “major questions” or questions of exceptional significance as a class warranting no deference because Congress would likely have insisted on maintaining control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 706 of the APA is indeterminate on deference
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 U.S.C. §706 does not prescribe either a deferential or de novo standard for reviewing agency statutory constructions; its command to “decide all relevant questions of law” is compatible with courts applying a reasonableness (deferential) review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: §706 neither mandates nor forbids Chevron-style deference; historical and scholarly readings (Jaffe, Davis, contemporaneous practice) treated Section 706 as compatible with reasonableness review. Courts that defer still ‘decide’ relevant questions by determining whether the agency stayed within the bounds of its assigned discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness policing function of courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when courts defer, they retain a policing role to ensure the agency acts within a zone of reasonable options—i.e., that the agency’s construction is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should review whether the agency has ‘stayed within the bounds of its assigned discretion’ and conform to Section 706 by determining whether agency constructions are reasonable rather than substituting their own judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis weight for Chevron
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron is entitled to strong stare decisis protection because of its long tenure, pervasive reliance by courts and parties, and the availability of legislative correction (Congress can alter the rule if it wishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overruling Chevron requires an exceptionally strong justification: the dissent emphasizes reliance interests (thousands of cases, major reliance by regulated parties), Congress’s repeated choice not to abolish Chevron, and the doctrine’s deep embedding in administrative law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional acquiescence as evidence of the correct default
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress’s long failure to enact a comprehensive abolition of Chevron or to insert contrary interpretive assignments in statutory drafting suggests legislative acceptance of Chevron’s presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legislative behavior (reauthorizations, failure to pass bills abolishing Chevron) as indicia that the Chevron presumption aligns with legislative intent; few targeted statutory exceptions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-APA and early-APA judicial practice favored deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical practice—cases like Gray v. Powell and NLRB v. Hearst Publications—and contemporaneous administrative-practice reports show that courts routinely gave weight to agency constructions prior to and contemporaneous with the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: because §706 was intended to ‘restate the present law,’ the pre-APA trend toward deference supports reading the APA as compatible with Chevron; earlier Supreme Court cases limited review to whether agency readings had ‘warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of institutional roles and democratic accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference reflects sensitivity to proper roles of political and judicial branches: agencies are politically accountable to the President and the public, and Congress delegated policymaking authority to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an interpretive choice is a policy trade-off better suited to a politically accountable agency (rather than a judge), give agencies primary authority; courts should respect institutional competencies and democratic accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity triggers are common and not proof of Chevron’s unworkability
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation in judges’ assessments of ambiguity does not render Chevron unworkable—ambiguity-based triggers are routine across legal doctrines and manageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: contract law, rule of lenity, constitutional avoidance, and other doctrines routinely confront ambiguity; the existence of interpretive disagreement elsewhere does not justify discarding Chevron.
